text:
Evidence supports the ingredients, but I found no direct study isolating recency-weighted versus unweighted BPR and BPR-max in recurrent recommendation with identical samplers. [Hidasi and Karatzoglou (2018)](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf) establish BPR-max’s emphasis on high-scoring negatives and explain ordinary BPR’s gradient dilution with many easy negatives. Their experiments examine loss–sampling interactions; this is distinct from weighting recent positive targets. [Petrov and Macdonald (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643) demonstrate effective recency-based training-sequence sampling, including for GRU4Rec, providing related evidence rather than a controlled test of the proposed loss weighting.

Recency gains are not universal. [Oh and Cho (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) report that excessive recency bias can impair recommendation accuracy and representation of long-term interests, with mitigation improving evaluated models. This does not directly establish that recency-weighted BPR causes those failures. Likewise, popularity-based negative sampling and popularity bias in recommendations are different quantities; weighting’s effect on recommendation popularity needs measurement.

The most informative next control is therefore a fixed-GRU4Rec 2×2 comparison: BPR/BPR-max × uniform/recency target weights, keeping sampled positives, negative candidates, initialization, updates and evaluation fixed. Normalize weights over valid targets to preserve average loss scale. Report the weighting gain within each loss and their interaction, alongside effective sample size, ESS=(Σw)²/Σw², target popularity exposure, recommendation popularity/coverage, and validation HR@10 by history length. ESS is a weight-concentration diagnostic, not an independent-sample count for correlated sequences. This experimental recommendation is an inference from the evidence; an architecture switch would not resolve the weighting hypothesis.
